opus-5.5.text:
That's a question I think about a lot, partly because watching children learn is humbling for someone who builds robots.

The biggest difference is how a child learns. A baby isn't handed a dataset. They explore: they put everything in their mouth, drop a spoon off the high chair fifty times, crawl, fall, get up. That play is self-directed and embodied. They're building an intuitive model of physics, of their own body, and of other people, all at once, and they're remarkably data-efficient. A toddler sees a cup knocked over a few times and understands it. A robot might need thousands or millions of trials, often in simulation, to learn something comparable.

There's also the developmental order. Children don't learn everything at once. They learn to hold their head up, then sit, crawl, stand, walk, and only later do fine manipulation and language. Each stage builds a foundation for the next. Robotics has historically done the opposite: we pick one narrow task, like grasping or walking, and optimize hard for it in isolation. Recently, with large foundation models and vision-language-action models, we're starting to see something closer to building general knowledge first and then grounding it in specific skills. But it's still not the gradual, curriculum-like unfolding a child goes through.

Then there's the body. A child's body is soft, compliant, full of sensors, and incredibly forgiving. They fall all the time and it's fine. Robots are rigid, expensive, and fragile in a different way. If a robot falls, something breaks, and someone has to fix it. That's a big reason we lean so heavily on simulation. It lets the robot "fall" millions of times safely. In a sense, simulation is our substitute for the safe, forgiving childhood that robots don't get to have.

Interestingly, the comparison has also become a bit inverted. Today's large models learn a lot of "common sense" from internet-scale text and video before they ever touch the physical world. That's almost backwards from a child, who learns physical common sense first and abstract knowledge later. So our robots can sometimes reason about a kitchen quite well and still be clumsy at actually picking up a slippery cup. That's a version of Moravec's paradox: what's easy for a two-year-old is still hard for us.

So I see children as an existence proof and a source of inspiration. They show that a general, adaptive, embodied intelligence can emerge from curiosity, interaction, and a good body. We're not trying to copy child development step by step, but many of the ideas, like curriculum learning, intrinsic motivation, learning from play, and learning by imitating others, came straight from looking at how kids do it. And honestly, we still have a lot to learn from them.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I think about a lot, actually, because the contrast is really striking once you look at it closely.

A child learns almost entirely through interaction with the physical world. They don't get a dataset. They fall down hundreds of times learning to walk, they put things in their mouth, they knock over cups, and every one of those "failures" is actually information. And crucially, nobody is standing over them with a precise reward function. The signal is very sparse, very noisy, and yet within a couple of years a toddler has a model of physics, of objects, of their own body, that is far more general than anything we can give a robot today.

Robots, by contrast, have historically learned in a very narrow way. Either we hand-engineer the controller, or we train in simulation on a very specific task with a very carefully shaped reward. The robot might become extremely good at that one thing, say walking on flat ground, and then you put a small rock in front of it and it completely falls apart. A two-year-old would just step over the rock without thinking.

So I'd say the biggest differences are three things. First, the breadth of experience. A child's "training data" is unbelievably diverse, continuous, and embodied. Second, the efficiency. Children learn from very few examples, whereas our reinforcement learning methods often need millions of trials, which is why we rely so heavily on simulation. And third, the way knowledge builds on itself. A child's skills compound: crawling leads to standing, standing leads to walking, walking leads to running and climbing. Most robot learning is still relatively siloed, each task started more or less from scratch.

What's exciting to me is that the gap is starting to close. With large pretrained models, robots can now inherit a huge amount of prior knowledge about the world before they ever take a step, a bit like how a child is born with certain innate structure and then refines it through experience. And with sim-to-real techniques, we can give a robot something closer to that childhood, lots of varied, messy experience, but compressed into hours instead of years.

So I don't think robots will learn exactly the way children do, and maybe they shouldn't. But children are the best existence proof we have that general, robust, embodied intelligence can emerge from interaction with the world, and that's the direction we're trying to push.

astra-6.text:
Children are remarkable learners. They learn by exploring, watching other people, and interacting with the world. A child trying to pick up a toy is learning about vision, touch, balance, and how objects behave—all at the same time. And those experiences become a foundation for learning new skills.

With robots, we usually make the problem much narrower. We might train a robot to walk or grasp an object, and it can become very good at that particular task. But that doesn’t necessarily mean it can use what it learned to solve a different problem. It also often needs much more training experience than a child would.

One advantage we have with robots is simulation. We can train many virtual robots in parallel, letting them practice and make mistakes without damaging hardware. But transferring that learning into the real world is still challenging.

So I think children offer an important inspiration: learning should be continuous, grounded in interaction, and useful across many tasks. We’ve made progress with individual robot skills, but that broader ability to learn and adapt is still a big gap.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the biggest difference is that children learn continuously through interaction with the world. They move, they play, they fall down, and they try again. They also build on what they’ve already learned, so each new skill doesn’t start from zero.

With robots, we usually make the problem much more structured. We define a task, design a training process, and give the robot feedback about how well it’s doing. It may become very good at that particular task, but transferring that ability to a new situation is still difficult.

There’s also the question of how much experience you need. A child can learn a lot from relatively few attempts. A robot may need a huge number of trials, which is one reason simulation is so useful: it lets us generate experience without repeatedly damaging the hardware.

So children give us a very compelling example of what we’d like to achieve—learning that is flexible, efficient, and grounded in physical interaction. But reproducing that in robots is still a big challenge.
